faq.q: Why is a single dose of albendazole sufficient?

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer presents with fatigue and hemoglobin 8 g/dL; what is your next diagnostic step — stool microscopy to look for hookworm eggs because anemia in this setting is most likely due to intestinal blood loss.
How does the life cycle of Necator americanus explain the importance of footwear — larvae penetrate skin; wearing shoes blocks entry, breaking transmission.

A child with iron‑deficiency anemia and a history of walking barefoot tests negative on a single stool smear; what should you do — repeat stool exam with concentration technique or treat empirically if high clinical suspicion.
Why is albendazole preferred over mebendazole for mass deworming campaigns — higher single‑dose cure rate, easier logistics, and lower risk of resistance.
What are the key features that differentiate hookworm‑related anemia from anemia of chronic disease — low ferritin, microcytic hypochromic indices, and exposure history.
A patient with severe anemia (< 7 g/dL) needs urgent care; what is the priority before deworming — stabilize with blood transfusion, then give albendazole once hemodynamically stable.
Explain why iron supplementation should follow, not precede, deworming — treating the parasite first stops ongoing blood loss; iron given before may be wasted and exacerbate gut irritation.
In a low‑resource clinic without microscopy, how can you support a presumptive diagnosis — use epidemiologic clues (barefoot, endemic area) and anemia labs, then treat with albendazole empirically.
ai.title: Necator americanus Infection
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Hookworm Necator americanus causes chronic intestinal blood loss leading to iron‑deficiency anemia and gastrointestinal discomfort. Diagnosis relies on stool microscopy, and treatment is with benzimidazoles. Prevention focuses on sanitation and footwear.

b: Adult worms reside in the duodenal mucosa
Life cycle requires warm, moist soil for larval development
sections.p: Necator americanus is a soil‑transmitted helminth endemic in tropical and subtropical low‑resource regions, especially East Africa. Infection is acquired through skin contact with contaminated soil.

b: Filariform (infective) third‑stage larvae (L3) are the stage that penetrates human skin
Adults attach to intestinal villi and feed on blood
sections.p: A slender, reddish‑brown nematode about 8‑13 mm long. Larvae possess a buccal capsule with cutting plates that penetrate skin.

b: Key risk factors: walking barefoot, use of night soil as fertilizer, poor sanitation
sections.p: Eggs passed in feces hatch in soil, develop to L3 larvae over 5‑7 days, then penetrate bare feet. Larvae travel via bloodstream to the lungs, ascend the bronchial tree, are swallowed, and mature in the small intestine.

b: Anemia severity graded by hemoglobin: mild 10‑12 g/dL, moderate 7‑9 g/dL, severe < 7 g/dL
Complications: cardiac strain from chronic anemia, susceptibility to other infections
sections.p: Chronic intestinal blood loss produces iron‑deficiency anemia; mild abdominal pain, dyspepsia, and occasional diarrhea may occur. Heavy infections can cause severe anemia, growth retardation in children, and reduced work capacity in adults.
Microscopic detection of characteristic oval eggs in a single stool sample is the mainstay. In low‑resource settings, concentration techniques improve yield.

t.b: Confirms presence of hookworm eggs; a positive result confirms infection. If unavailable, consider a clinical diagnosis in endemic area with anemia and exposure history.
Assesses anemia severity; guides urgency of treatment and need for transfusion.
Distinguishes iron‑deficiency anemia from anemia of chronic disease; low ferritin supports hookworm‑related loss.

b: Iron tablets (ferrous sulfate) for 3 months after deworming
Health education: wear shoes, avoid night soil, improve latrine use
sections.p: Single‑dose benzimidazole therapy eradicates adult worms; iron supplementation corrects anemia. Community measures reduce reinfection.

b: In endemic areas, any iron‑deficiency anemia in a barefoot adult warrants a stool exam for hookworm.
Albendazole is preferred over mebendazole because of higher cure rates and single‑dose convenience.
Severe anemia (< 7 g/dL) requires urgent transfusion before deworming.
sections.p: Focus on epidemiology, anemia work‑up, and appropriate deworming regimen. Remember that stool microscopy may be negative in light infections; clinical suspicion remains key.

whenToSeekHelp: Hemoglobin < 7 g/dL or symptomatic cardiac failure
Signs of severe malnutrition in children
